body:
Glaciers as natural freshwater reservoirs

Mountain glaciers store water in the form of ice and release meltwater, particularly during warmer months. This helps sustain river flow during periods when other sources of water may be limited.

The Himalayan and Karakoram mountain systems contain important glaciers that contribute water to the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra drainage systems. Their contribution varies between river basins and seasons because Himalayan rivers also receive water from rainfall and seasonal snowmelt.

Important Indian glaciers and river associations

GlacierLocationAssociated river
GangotriUttarakhandBhagirathi
AlkapuriUttarakhandAlaknanda
ChorabariUttarakhandMandakini
MilamUttarakhandGori Ganga
Bara ShigriHimachal PradeshChandra

The Bhagirathi emerges from the Gangotri Glacier at Gaumukh. It joins the Alaknanda at Devprayag, after which the combined river is known as the Ganga.

The Chandra is one of the principal headstreams of the Chenab, which belongs to the Indus drainage system. Thus, Bara Shigri Glacier is associated with the Indus river basin, whereas Gangotri and Alkapuri are associated with the Ganga basin.

Effects of climate warming on glaciers

Higher temperatures generally increase ablation and may reduce the amount of precipitation falling as snow. If accumulation fails to compensate for these losses, a glacier experiences negative mass balance.

Individual glaciers need not respond identically. Their responses also depend on snowfall, elevation, slope, debris cover and local climatic conditions.

Changes in river discharge

During the initial stages of sustained glacier mass loss, increased melting may temporarily increase meltwater discharge. However, continued shrinkage eventually reduces the amount of ice available to melt, potentially decreasing the glacier's contribution to rivers, especially during periods of low rainfall.

This transition from increasing to decreasing glacier runoff is commonly associated with the concept of peak water.

Sea-level rise

When land-based glaciers and ice sheets lose ice to the oceans, they add water to the oceans and contribute to global sea-level rise.

Melting floating sea ice has comparatively little direct effect on sea level because it already displaces approximately the amount of water corresponding to its mass.

Ice-albedo feedback

Snow and ice reflect a relatively large proportion of incoming solar radiation. This reflectivity is called albedo. When snow and ice retreat, darker rock, soil or water may become exposed. These surfaces absorb more solar energy, encouraging further warming and melting.

Glacial lake outburst floods

A Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) is a sudden release of water from a lake associated with a glacier, often following the failure or overtopping of an ice or moraine dam.

Retreating glaciers may leave depressions filled with meltwater. Natural dams of loose rock debris or ice can retain large volumes of water. Landslides, avalanches and other disturbances may generate waves, cause overtopping or destabilise the dam.

The resulting flood can carry enormous quantities of water and sediment into downstream valleys, damaging settlements, bridges, roads and hydropower infrastructure.

South Lhonak Lake, Sikkim

On 4 October 2023, a glacial lake outburst flood originating from South Lhonak Lake affected the Teesta River valley in Sikkim. It caused extensive damage to downstream infrastructure, including the hydropower project at Chungthang.

Satellite monitoring of glacial lakes, assessment of natural dams, early-warning systems and risk-sensitive planning can reduce downstream vulnerability.

Prelims focus

  • Gangotri Glacier supplies the Bhagirathi; Alkapuri supplies the Alaknanda.
  • The Bhagirathi and Alaknanda meet at Devprayag.
  • Bara Shigri Glacier is associated with the Chandra River in Himachal Pradesh.
  • Land-based ice loss contributes to sea-level rise.
  • South Lhonak Lake, Sikkim, is associated with the 4 October 2023 Teesta flood.
  • Trap: Glacier shrinkage does not necessarily cause an immediate reduction in meltwater discharge.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, p. 66, online copy; National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research, Glaciological Monitoring of Benchmark Glaciers of Chandra Basin; Kumaon Mandal Vikas Nigam, Milam Glacier; Ministry of Water Resources, Flood in Catchment Area of Gandhi Sarovar, 12 August 2013; IPCC, Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate, 2019, Chapter 2; Government of Sikkim, Post Disaster Needs Assessment: Glacial Lake Outburst Flood Sikkim 2023, Section 6.2, pp. 184–185; online sources consulted 28 November 2026.]

body:
Meaning of periglacial environments

Periglacial environments are cold regions where ground freezing, thawing and frost-related processes play an important role in shaping the landscape. They may occur near glaciers, but they are not restricted to areas immediately surrounding glaciers.

Unlike glacial landforms, which are principally produced by moving ice masses, periglacial landforms commonly result from the freezing and thawing of water within soil, sediment and rock.

Permafrost and the active layer

Permafrost is ground consisting of soil, sediment or rock that remains at or below 0°C for at least 2 consecutive years.

Permafrost is defined by ground temperature rather than by the presence of visible ice. Some permafrost contains large quantities of ground ice, while relatively dry rock can also qualify as permafrost if it satisfies the temperature and duration conditions.

Permafrost is widespread in high-latitude regions such as Siberia, northern Canada and Alaska. It also occurs at high elevations in the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau.

Active layer

The active layer is the ground above permafrost that thaws during the warmer season and freezes again during the colder season. Water released during seasonal thawing may accumulate because the underlying frozen ground restricts downward drainage.

Ground that freezes in winter but thaws completely during summer is seasonally frozen ground. It is not necessarily permafrost.

Important periglacial processes

Frost weathering

Water enters cracks in rocks and freezes when the temperature falls sufficiently. Repeated freezing and thawing can widen fractures and break rocks into smaller, often angular fragments. This mechanical weathering is important in cold mountain environments.

Frost heave and patterned ground

Ice formation within soil can raise or displace the ground. This process is called frost heave. Repeated freezing, thawing and particle sorting may arrange stones and finer material into distinctive circles, polygons or stripes known as patterned ground.

Solifluction

During seasonal thawing, the upper soil layer may become saturated with water while the ground beneath remains frozen. The wet material moves slowly downhill under gravity, producing lobes or terraces. This slow movement of water-saturated soil is called solifluction.

Pingos and thermokarst

A pingo is a mound or hill containing a core of ground ice. It develops when water freezes within the ground and expansion associated with ice accumulation raises the overlying surface.

Thermokarst develops when ice-rich permafrost thaws and the ground loses volume or support. Surface subsidence may produce irregular depressions and thaw lakes.

Permafrost thaw and climate change

Permafrost can preserve considerable quantities of organic matter because low temperatures slow microbial decomposition. When the ground thaws, microorganisms can break down this organic material and release greenhouse gases.

  • Carbon dioxide: Released during microbial decomposition, especially under oxygen-rich conditions.
  • Methane: Can be produced in oxygen-poor, waterlogged environments.

These greenhouse gases can contribute to further atmospheric warming, encouraging additional permafrost thaw. This is a positive climate feedback.

Thawing ice-rich ground may also destabilise buildings, roads and slopes, damage pipelines and alter the drainage of lakes and wetlands. In high mountains, thawing frozen ground can contribute to rockfalls and slope instability.

Thermokarst and limestone karst

Thermokarst develops primarily through thawing ground ice and surface subsidence. Limestone karst develops primarily through the chemical dissolution of soluble rock. Their depressions may look similar, but their formation processes differ.

Prelims focus

  • Permafrost remains at or below 0°C for at least 2 consecutive years.
  • The active layer freezes and thaws seasonally.
  • Permafrost occurs in both polar and high-altitude regions.
  • Solifluction involves the slow downslope movement of saturated soil.
  • Pingos contain ground ice; thermokarst results from thaw-related subsidence.
  • Trap: The presence of visible ice is not a necessary condition for permafrost.

[References: National Snow and Ice Data Center, Frozen Ground and Permafrost, sections What Is Permafrost and Where Is Permafrost Located; National Snow and Ice Data Center, Does Permafrost Thaw Contribute to Global Warming?, updated 26 October 2020; AntarcticGlaciers.org, Periglacial Landforms; IPCC, Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability, Technical Summary; consulted 28 November 2026.]

title: Permafrost and Periglacial Landforms

body:
Wind as a geomorphic agent

Processes and landforms produced by wind are described as aeolian or eolian. Wind can remove loose material, transport sediment and deposit it in new locations.

Wind action is particularly effective in arid and semi-arid environments because these regions frequently have sparse vegetation, exposed soil, dry sediment and strong winds. However, aeolian processes also operate along sandy coasts, river floodplains and other locations with exposed sediment.

Water remains an important geomorphic agent in deserts. Occasional intense rainfall can produce flash floods and sheet wash, which erode slopes and transport considerable quantities of sediment.

Major processes of wind erosion

Deflation

Deflation is the removal of loose surface particles by wind. Fine sediment is lifted and transported, while heavier fragments may remain behind. Prolonged deflation can lower the land surface and create shallow depressions known as deflation hollows or blowouts.

Abrasion or corrasion

Wind carrying sand particles can act like a natural sandblasting agent. The particles strike exposed rock surfaces and gradually wear them away.

The effectiveness of abrasion depends on wind speed, sediment supply, particle size and the resistance of the rock.

Attrition

Transported particles may collide with one another, becoming smaller or more rounded. This process is called attrition. Unlike abrasion of exposed bedrock, attrition principally modifies the transported sediment itself.

Modes of wind transportation

The movement of sediment by wind depends mainly on particle size and wind strength.

  • Suspension: Fine dust particles remain airborne and can be carried over long distances.
  • Saltation: Sand grains move in a series of short jumps or bounces close to the ground.
  • Surface creep: Relatively coarse grains roll or slide along the ground, sometimes pushed by the impact of saltating particles.

Saltation is especially important in the movement of sand and the development of dunes. Suspension allows finer particles to travel much farther and may eventually produce extensive deposits of windblown silt.

Desert pavements and major erosional landforms

Desert pavement

A desert pavement is a surface closely covered by gravel, pebbles and rock fragments. It can develop when deflation removes finer material and leaves a protective concentration of coarse particles. Dust accumulation beneath the stones and other soil-forming processes may also contribute to its development.

The coarse surface cover can protect underlying sediment against further wind erosion. A desert pavement is therefore different from a dune, which consists mainly of accumulated sand.

Mushroom or pedestal rock

Sand-laden winds often transport the greatest concentration of abrasive sand close to the ground. Together with differences in rock resistance, stronger abrasion of the lower portion of a rock may produce a narrow base supporting a broader upper portion. This form resembles a mushroom.

Yardang

A yardang is an elongated, streamlined ridge sculpted in exposed rock or compacted sediment. Persistent wind abrasion and deflation preferentially remove weaker material, leaving ridges generally aligned with the effective wind direction.

Ventifact

A ventifact is a stone shaped, polished or faceted by the impact of windblown particles. Its surfaces may provide evidence of prolonged wind abrasion.

Related arid-region landforms

A pediment is a gently inclined erosional rock surface at the foot of a mountain, sometimes covered by a thin layer of debris. Several pediments may merge to produce an extensive low-relief surface called a pediplain.

An isolated residual hill rising above such a surface is called an inselberg. Pediments and inselbergs develop through combinations of weathering and erosion, including water action; they are not exclusively products of wind erosion.

A playa is a low-lying basin floor where temporary water may accumulate and subsequently evaporate, leaving mud or salt deposits.

Prelims focus

  • Deflation removes loose particles; abrasion wears exposed surfaces.
  • Suspension carries fine dust, saltation moves sand, and creep moves relatively coarse particles.
  • Desert pavements consist largely of closely packed coarse rock fragments.
  • Yardangs are generally elongated along the effective wind direction.
  • Pediments are gently sloping erosional surfaces at mountain foothills.
  • Trap: Wind is not the only important erosional agent in deserts.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19, Chapter 3, Work of Wind; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, Winds, printed pp. 71–73, online copy; U.S. Geological Survey, Eolian Processes; U.S. National Park Service, Nicholas Lancaster, Monitoring Aeolian Features and Processes, sections Transport of Particles by Wind and Wind Erosion; consulted 28 November 2026.]
